title: The super funds thriving over 10 years
full_text:
With FY26 returns now finalised, Chant West and SuperRatings have revealed the super funds that have delivered the strongest long-term returns over the past decade.
Analysis from Chant West and SuperRatings found super funds generated another year of strong returns despite geopolitical conflict, inflation pressures and bouts of market volatility, before highlighting the funds that have produced the strongest long-term outcomes over the past decade.
Chant West estimated the median growth fund, with between 61 per cent and 80 per cent invested in growth assets, returned 9.5 per cent in FY26.
The result marked a fourth consecutive year of returns above 9 per cent, following gains of 9.2 per cent in FY23, 9.1 per cent in FY24 and 10.4 per cent in FY25, lifting cumulative returns to 44 per cent over four years.
SuperRatings similarly estimated the median balanced option returned 9.4 per cent in FY26, down from 10.3 per cent a year earlier but with every balanced option expected to finish the year in positive territory.
Chant West head of super investment Mano Mohankumar said hedged international shares returned 25.5 per cent during FY26, while unhedged international shares gained 17 per cent despite the Australian dollar appreciating against most major currencies.
“Generally speaking, the better performing funds were those that had higher allocations to international shares, particularly where a larger proportion of that exposure was currency hedged,” Mohankumar said.
He said diversification also benefited members, with international listed infrastructure and international listed property returning 17.2 per cent and 14.3 per cent respectively, while Australian listed property was the only major asset class to record a negative return, falling 1.8 per cent.
As for how this year’s performance translates into long-term performance, both research houses published their data for fund performance over the last 10 years.
SuperRatings’ balanced fund survey ranked Hostplus as the strongest-performing balanced option over the 10 years to 30 June 2026, delivering 8.9 per cent per annum.
Brighter Super followed on 8.8 per cent, while Hostplus’ Indexed Balanced option and Australian Retirement Trust each returned 8.7 per cent per annum. AustralianSuper rounded out the top five with an annualised return of 8.5 per cent.
Source: SuperRatings/Chant West, July 2026
Rappell said the decade-long results demonstrated the value of maintaining a long-term investment strategy.
“This year has been another strong result, well above the long-term annual return of 7.3 per cent since compulsory superannuation began in 1992. Converted into dollars, $100 invested in the median balanced super fund in 1992 would now be worth over 10 times that amount at approximately $1,099,” he said.
Looking into FY27
Both research houses expect investment conditions to remain volatile in FY27 as markets continue to contend with geopolitical uncertainty, inflation and questions over the long-term impact of artificial intelligence on economic growth.
Rappell said navigating those periods of uncertainty was one of the key responsibilities of superannuation investment teams.
“Protecting member balances from larger moves in markets is a key function of superannuation investment teams, and the importance of this role only grows as members approach the end of their working life,” he said.
“While funds that were more defensively positioned have not benefited as much from the growth that markets have delivered in recent years, strong diversification helps shelter members from market fluctuations and supports smoother returns over the long term.”
Mohankumar said the past four years of returns above 9 per cent should not be viewed as the new benchmark for investors.
“The typical long-term return objective for growth funds is to beat inflation by 3.5 per cent p.a., which translates to roughly 6 per cent p.a.,” he said.
“Since the introduction of compulsory super, the annualised return is 8 per cent and the annual CPI increase is 2.7 per cent, giving a real return of 5.3 per cent p.a. – well above that 3.5 per cent target.”
author: Adrian Suljanovic
